section.title: The LORD's Answer and the Five Woes
section.sectionRationale: This is the heart of the book and the answer to both of the prophet's complaints. God tells Habakkuk to write the vision and wait for it, gives the line that will shape the whole New Testament gospel, the righteous will live by faith, and then pronounces five woes on the proud oppressor, promising that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of His glory and that all the earth must fall silent before Him.
section.thesis: God answers that the vision has an appointed time, that the proud will collapse under their own arrogance while the righteous will live by faith, and that Babylon and every proud power stands under woe, for the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.
section.frameNote: Four movements: write the vision and wait for the appointed time; the contrast of the proud and the righteous who lives by faith; the five woes against greed, injustice, bloodshed, cruelty, and idolatry; and the closing call, the LORD is in His holy temple, let all the earth be silent.

units.label: Write the vision, wait for it

verses.text: Then the LORD answered me: “Write down this {{chazon|vision}} and clearly inscribe it on tablets, so that a herald may run with it.
For the vision awaits an appointed time; it testifies of the end and does not lie. Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay.

units.label: The proud and the righteous
units.note: the righteous will live by faith

verses.text: Look at the proud one; his soul is not upright, but the righteous will live by {{emunah|faith}}.

and wealth indeed betrays him. He is an arrogant man never at rest. He enlarges his appetite like Sheol, and like Death, he is never satisfied. He gathers all the nations to himself and collects all the peoples as his own.

Will not all of these take up a taunt against him, speaking with mockery and derision: ‘{{hoy|Woe}} to him who amasses what is not his and makes himself rich with many loans! How long will this go on?’
Will not your creditors suddenly arise and those who disturb you awaken? Then you will become their prey.
Because you have plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder you, because of your bloodshed against man and your violence against the land, the city, and all their dwellers.
Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain, to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster!
You have plotted shame for your house by cutting off many peoples and forfeiting your life.
For the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork.
Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town by iniquity!
Is it not indeed from the LORD of Hosts that the labor of the people only feeds the fire, and the nations weary themselves in vain?
For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the {{kavod|glory}} of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
Woe to him who gives drink to his neighbors, pouring it from the wineskin until they are drunk, in order to gaze at their nakedness!
You will be filled with shame instead of glory. You too must drink and expose your uncircumcision! The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you, and utter disgrace will cover your glory.

For your violence against Lebanon will overwhelm you, and the destruction of animals will terrify you, because of your bloodshed against men and your violence against the land, the city, and all their dwellers.
What use is an {{elil|idol}}, that a craftsman should carve it, or an image, a teacher of lies? For its maker trusts in his own creation; he makes idols that cannot speak.
Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ or to silent stone, ‘Arise!’ Can it give guidance? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, yet there is no breath in it at all.”

units.label: Silence before the LORD
units.note: He is in His holy temple

verses.text: But the LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him.

chazon.gloss: A vision or revelation, a word seen and received from God. Habakkuk is told to write the chazon plainly on tablets so a herald can run with it. It is a sure prophetic word with an appointed time, meant to be published and trusted while God's people wait for it to come to pass.

emunah.gloss: Faithfulness, steadfastness, and so faith: firm trust that holds fast to God. The word carries both leaning on God and being loyal to Him. In 2:4 the righteous live by emunah, trusting God's promise while they wait; the New Testament draws out that this trust, not human achievement, is how a person is justified before God.

hoy.gloss: Woe, an anguished cry of warning and lament, like alas or ah. It opens each of the five taunts against the oppressor. A hoy is a funeral-like announcement of coming judgment: the proud plunderer is as good as dead, and creation itself will testify against him.

kavod.gloss: Glory, weight, honor, the visible splendor of God's presence. The promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD is the high point of the chapter: every proud empire will pass, but God's glory will flood the whole world as surely as water fills the sea.

elil.gloss: An idol, a worthless thing, a nothing. The word is deliberately dismissive: idols are empty, powerless, and mute. The last woe exposes the folly of trusting what human hands have made, a teacher of lies with no breath in it, in contrast to the living LORD in His holy temple.

basic.context: This is God's full answer to Habakkuk. First, God tells him to write the vision clearly so it can be passed on, and to wait for it, because it will certainly come at the right time. Then comes the pivotal line: the proud will not endure, but the righteous will live by faith. After that, God pronounces five woes on the arrogant oppressor for greed, dishonest gain, bloodshed, cruelty, and idolatry, promising that one day the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of His glory, and calling all the earth to fall silent before Him.
basic.hermeneutics: Verse 4 is the hinge of the whole book and one of the most important sentences in the Bible. In its setting it means that while the proud Babylonian trusts his own strength, God's people are to survive the crisis by trusting God and His promise. The New Testament takes up this same principle and shows its full depth: a person is made right with God not by works but by faith. The five woes are not random; they expose the way the proud life destroys itself and others.
basic.originalLanguages: God tells Habakkuk to write the chazon, the vision, a sure word with an appointed time. The proud man's soul is not upright, but the righteous will live by emunah, a word meaning both faith and faithfulness, a trust that holds on to God. Each judgment opens with hoy, woe, a funeral cry. The chapter peaks on kavod, the glory of the LORD, filling the earth, and ends by exposing the elil, the worthless idol, with no breath in it.
basic.typology: The vision that waits for an appointed time and will surely come points to the coming of Christ and, beyond, to His return; Hebrews applies the words to the one who is coming and will not delay. The cup of God's wrath passed to the oppressor is the cup Jesus drinks in the place of His people. And the earth filled with God's glory anticipates the new creation.
basic.christ: The righteous will live by faith becomes the banner text of the gospel: Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 to prove that we are justified by faith in Christ alone, and Hebrews 10:38 uses it to urge perseverance. Jesus is both the righteous one who lived by perfect faith and the one who drank the cup of wrath so that the earth might be filled with the knowledge of God's glory in His face.
basic.god: We learn that God keeps His word on His own perfect schedule, that He is patient but never idle, that He hates greed, violence, exploitation, and idolatry, and that He is supremely committed to His own glory filling the whole earth. He is the living God in His holy temple before whom every proud mouth must finally fall silent.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, and Hebrews 10:37 to 38 all take up 2:4. Isaiah 11:9 parallels the earth filled with the knowledge of the LORD. Revelation 14 and 16 pick up the cup of wrath and the fall of Babylon.
basic.oneStory: At the center of the book God reveals how His people survive judgment and how sinners are saved in every age: not by their own strength, which is doomed, but by faith. That single line runs straight into the New Testament gospel, and the promise of the earth filled with God's glory carries the story all the way to the new creation.

context.literary:
God's answer in this passage is built in three layers. The first, verses 2 and 3, is a commission about the word itself: how it is to be written, who is to carry it and how long it will take. The second, verses 4 and 5, is a hinge that sets two kinds of person side by side, the one whose soul is 'not upright' and the one who lives. The third, verses 6 to 20, is a long taunt that falls into five woes, each followed by a reason that begins with 'for' or 'because.'

The five woes are carefully paired with their own punishments, and the pairing is the heart of the structure. The one who 'amasses what is not his' is met by creditors who rise up, verses 6 and 7. The one who builds his house by unjust gain hears his own stones cry out, verses 9 to 11. The one who builds a city by bloodshed finds that the labour of the peoples only 'feeds the fire,' verses 12 and 13. The one who gives his neighbours drink to gaze at their nakedness is made to drink the cup himself and be exposed, verses 15 and 16. And the one who makes a wooden god and says 'Awake!' finds there is no breath in it, verses 18 and 19. In each case the sin is turned back on the sinner in its own form.

Two verses break the pattern, and they are the theological peaks. Verse 14 comes after the woe on the bloody city: 'the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.' Verse 20 closes the whole oracle after the woe on idols: 'the LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him.' The first answers the empire's attempt to fill the earth with its own power, and the second answers the idol's silence with the silence of those who face the living God. The woes are not dark for their own sake. They are the contrasts that make the glory visible.

The speaker of the taunt is also notable. Verse 6 asks, 'Will not all of these take up a taunt against him?' The 'all of these' are the nations he has plundered. The dirge is sung by the victims, and God has given them the words. The final unity is that the passage begins with the prophet's fear that God is silent, and ends with God commanding silence of everyone else.
context.historical:
The woes are aimed at a Babylon whose economy and ambitions the first hearers could see. The empire's building programme in its capital was lavish, and its wealth was supported by the labour and tribute of conquered peoples. Verse 9, where the proud builder places 'his nest on high' to 'escape the hand of disaster,' catches the instinct of every power that thinks wealth and height can keep it safe. Obadiah had said the same of Edom: 'Though you soar like the eagle and make your nest among the stars, even from there I will bring you down,' Obadiah 1:4.

The language of debt in verses 6 and 7 has a legal and social background. Israel's law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite, Exodus 22:25, and set limits on taking pledges, Deuteronomy 24:10 to 13. A nation that builds its wealth by loans and pledges extracts from the weak what the covenant would protect. The Hebrew word for a creditor is literally 'one who bites,' and it comes from the same root as the word for interest, so the image of verse 7 is of biters who awake and bite back.

The accusation of verse 17, 'your violence against Lebanon,' refers to the forests of Lebanon, whose cedars were cut for the building of palaces and temples. Isaiah gives the other side: the cypresses and cedars of Lebanon rejoice when Babylon's king is laid low, 'no woodcutter comes against us,' Isaiah 14:8. The same Babylon that ruined Judah's people also stripped the land.

The idol polemic in verses 18 to 20 belongs to a long Israelite tradition of mockery. Jeremiah, Isaiah and the Psalms all describe idols as things that cannot speak, walk or breathe, Jeremiah 10:5, Isaiah 44:9 to 10, Psalm 135:15 to 18. Babylon's religion was built around images, and Habakkuk's hearers faced the daily pressure to consider those gods stronger than the LORD because their worshippers were winning.

The audience, in short, were people for whom the question 'how long?' meant exile. The vision was meant to be carried by a herald through a nation in crisis, in the hope that it would reach people before the army did.
context.canonical:
The commission to 'write down this vision and clearly inscribe it on tablets' has deep roots. The verb for 'clearly' is the one Moses used when the law was to be written on the stones at Mount Ebal, 'write distinctly upon these stones all the words of this law,' Deuteronomy 27:8. Isaiah is told to 'write it on a tablet' and 'inscribe it on a scroll' so that it will be a witness for days to come, Isaiah 30:8. Habakkuk's oracle is put in the same category: a word to be recorded for those who will need it later.

Verse 4 is the book's centre of gravity and one of the most influential lines in the New Testament. Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17 as the summary of his gospel, 'The righteous will live by faith,' and again in Galatians 3:11 to prove that no one is justified before God by the law. The author of Hebrews uses it as an encouragement to endure, quoting it together with verse 3: 'In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay. But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him,' Hebrews 10:37 to 38. Three New Testament writers take the same line in three directions, justification, the relation of faith to law, and endurance.

Genesis 15:6 stands behind it: 'Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.' Paul draws that link in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6 to 9. The principle that Habakkuk states for his generation is the principle of Abraham's own standing before God.

The knowledge of God's glory covering the earth in verse 14 echoes earlier texts. The LORD swears, 'as surely as the whole earth is filled with the glory of the LORD,' Numbers 14:21. Isaiah hears the seraphim cry that 'all the earth is full of His glory,' Isaiah 6:3, and the psalmist prays for the same, Psalm 72:19. Isaiah 11:9 says the earth 'will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water.' Habakkuk blends these and adds the word 'glory.'

The cup of verse 16 belongs with Psalm 75:8, Isaiah 51:17 to 23 and Jeremiah 25:15 to 29. Revelation takes it up when Babylon is given 'the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath,' Revelation 16:19. Jesus Himself prays about the cup in Gethsemane, Matthew 26:39, and tells Peter, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Habakkuk wanted his hearers to believe that God's answer was both sure and slow, and to know what to do while they waited. The instruction to write the vision, to have it carried, and then to wait for what lingers is a plan for living in the gap between promise and fulfilment. His readers could not see the end of Babylon. They were to trust that it would come and that the word would not lie.

He also meant to show what two kinds of life look like. The proud man is not upright, his wealth betrays him, his appetite has no bottom. The righteous person lives by trust. The contrast is not about two personalities but about two directions of dependence: one on the self, one on God. The five woes then show where the first direction leads, so that the hearers can choose which they are walking.

Finally, he intended to console the afflicted and to warn the powerful in the same words. The afflicted hear that every wrong has a reckoning, and that the day will come when the whole earth knows the glory of God. The powerful hear that gain taken by loan, by violence or by deceit will be answered. And everyone hears that before the living God, all voices must stop. This is an oracle for those with little power, written so that they might not lose heart, and it is a moral standard for those with much.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The five woes describe how God judges a certain kind of life, and one empire in particular. They are not a series of laws, though they imply a standard: do not enrich yourself by what is not yours, do not build with injustice, do not found cities on blood, do not humiliate your neighbours, do not worship what you make. These apply to every age because the sins they describe are not limited to Babylon.

The statement that the righteous will live by faith is both a description and an invitation. In its setting it describes the way God's people will survive the coming invasion, by trusting Him rather than their own strength. Paul and the author of Hebrews carry it further by applying it to how a sinner is made right before God and to how a believer should endure. It is not a command that people earn life by a quantity of belief. It tells us the way of life in God's economy: by trust.

The instruction to wait is also not an excuse for passivity. The prophet is told to write, to have the word run, and to wait. A believer who reads that 'it will surely come' must not use the verse to justify idleness or to ignore the injustice in front of him. Waiting in the Bible is an active habit of trust, and the book will end, in chapter 3, with a prayer and a song that bring the waiting into worship.

debates.question: Does 'faith' in verse 4 mean trust in God or faithfulness to Him?

views.label: Trust in God's promise
views.case: The context is a word that tarries, and the call to 'wait for it.' The righteous person is the one who trusts that the vision will come. This is the way Paul and the Septuagint tradition lean, since they translate with the Greek word for faith, pistis, and Paul uses the line in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 to teach justification by faith. The contrast in the verse is with the proud man who trusts himself.

views.label: Faithfulness or steadfastness
views.case: The Hebrew noun, emunah, often means reliability or steadfastness, as in the hands of Moses that 'remained steady' until sunset, Exodus 17:12, and the BSB footnote says 'Or faithfulness.' On this reading, the righteous person lives by holding steady under pressure. The Hebrew carries a suffix, 'his' emunah, so it is the person's own steadfastness that is in view.

debates.bearing: The two views meet in the way biblical faith works: trust that holds firm. The New Testament does not abandon the Hebrew sense, since Hebrews 10:38 to 39 uses the verse to urge perseverance, and Paul's use in Romans keeps the emphasis on trust as the only way to life. In the gospel, the one who trusts is also made steadfast.

debates.question: Who or what is the one 'who is coming' in verse 3?

views.label: The vision itself
views.case: The grammar of verse 3 allows 'it' as the subject: the vision will surely come and will not delay. Habakkuk had asked about a word that tarries, and this answer says that the word has an appointed time. The BSB text takes this line.

views.label: A person who is coming
views.case: The BSB footnote notes the alternative, 'Though He lingers, wait for Him, since He will surely come and will not delay,' which also reflects the Septuagint. Hebrews 10:37 reads, 'He who is coming will come and will not delay,' and understands it of the Messiah. The Hebrew verbs are masculine singular and can refer to a person.

debates.bearing: The vision and the person are not rivals. The vision is the word of God's coming judgment and salvation, and the person is the one in whom that salvation arrives. Hebrews hears the verse as a promise about Christ's return, and its use fits the way the oracle points beyond the Babylonian crisis.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 commands that the vision be written 'clearly,' using a verb, ba'er, that means to make plain or distinct. It is the verb Moses uses of the law written on the plastered stones at Ebal, Deuteronomy 27:8. Habakkuk's vision is to have the clarity and the permanence of a law. The purpose clause, 'so that a herald may run with it,' is literally 'so that the one who reads it may run,' and it can be taken two ways. Either a reader can run with its meaning because it is so plain, or a messenger can run to deliver it. The plain script serves either.

Verse 3 says the vision 'awaits an appointed time,' mo'ed, the word for a fixed season or meeting, used of the festivals of Israel. It 'testifies of the end,' and the verb carries the sense of breathing out or declaring, a word used for a witness who speaks. The command 'wait for it' uses the verb chakah, to wait with expectation, as in Isaiah 30:18 and Isaiah 8:17. And the promise is said twice in a form that stresses certainty: 'it will surely come,' a repetition of the verb 'to come' in its emphatic form, 'and will not delay.' The Greek of Hebrews 10:37 renders it as a person, 'He who is coming,' and the Hebrew verbs are masculine, so the line can be heard either way.

In verse 4 the proud one's soul is 'not upright,' using the adjective yashar, straight or level. The righteous person lives by 'his' faith, a possessive that the BSB drops. The Septuagint reads 'my faith' or has God say 'My soul has no pleasure in him' of the one who draws back, as the BSB footnote records, and Hebrews 10:38 follows a version of that wording with 'My righteous one.' Paul in Romans 1:17 leaves out the possessive altogether and writes simply 'The righteous will live by faith.' The line was flexible enough in the first century for three writers to shape it to their needs without losing its core.

The footnote to verse 5 records a textual difference: the Masoretic Text has 'wine,' and the Dead Sea Scrolls have 'wealth.' The BSB follows the Scrolls: 'wealth indeed betrays him.' The image of the throat of Sheol and Death in the same verse recalls Isaiah 5:14, where Sheol 'enlarges its throat,' and Proverbs 27:20, where Sheol is never satisfied. The conqueror's appetite is as wide as the grave.

Verse 6 gives the form of the poem: the nations speak 'a taunt,' mashal, 'mockery,' and 'derision' or riddles. Isaiah 14:4 uses the same word of the song the exiles will sing against the king of Babylon. In verse 7 the creditors are 'those who bite you,' from the verb nashak, whose noun neshek is the ordinary word for interest. Those who bite will awake, and the debt-collector becomes the one who is bitten.

In verse 11 'the stones will cry out,' from the verb za'aq, the same verb as Habakkuk's own cry of 'Violence!' in 1:2. The prophet cried out and seemed not to be heard, and now the walls of the oppressor cry out for him.

In verse 16 the footnote says that the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint and the Syriac read 'and stagger' where the Hebrew text has 'and expose your uncircumcision.' The Hebrew words are alike in form, he'arel and hera'el, so a copyist's slip is easy to imagine. Either way the picture is of a drunkard who falls and is exposed.

The verbs of verse 18 reveal a pattern: the idol is called a 'teacher of lies,' moreh sheqer, and its maker 'trusts in his own creation,' from the root that forms a potter's clay figure, yatsar, the verb of Genesis 2:7 where God 'formed' man. The creature forms a god, and the Creator formed the creature. Verse 19 asks if the idol 'can give guidance,' using yoreh, from the same root as torah and moreh. The teacher of lies has no torah to give.

Verse 20 says 'be silent,' with the interjection has, a hush used also in Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13. It is the sound of a room that falls quiet when the king walks in.

typology.type: The vision that waits for its appointed time, Habakkuk 2:3
typology.fulfillment: The word that lingers and then comes is read by the author of Hebrews as a promise about Christ: 'In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay,' Hebrews 10:37. The correspondence is that the appointed time came for the first coming and is still to come for the second. Peter explains the delay: 'The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise... but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish,' 2 Peter 3:9. The escalation is that the vision is no longer a message about an empire but a person whose arrival is the end of the world's waiting. The type is incomplete until He returns.

typology.type: The cup in the LORD's right hand, Habakkuk 2:16
typology.fulfillment: The cup of wrath goes around the nations and comes to Babylon. Jesus takes up the cup in Gethsemane, 'let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and says, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11. The correspondence is in the cup of judgment from the hand of God. The escalation is that the Righteous One drinks what the guilty deserve, so that Isaiah's promise comes true: 'From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again,' Isaiah 51:22. Those who refuse Him will still drink it, Revelation 14:10.

typology.type: The stones that cry out, Habakkuk 2:11
typology.fulfillment: When the house of the unjust is made to testify against its builder, the creation itself bears witness. Jesus uses the image when the Pharisees try to silence the crowd on the road to Jerusalem: 'if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out,' Luke 19:40. The correspondence is that creation will speak when human witnesses are silenced. The escalation is that the stones in Luke cry out in praise of the King, not in accusation of a builder. The type falls short in that Habakkuk's stones indict, while in Luke's setting they would acclaim.

typology.type: The LORD in His holy temple, Habakkuk 2:20
typology.fulfillment: The oracle ends with God in His temple and the earth silent. In Christ the temple has a new meaning. Jesus speaks of 'the temple of His body,' John 2:21, and enters 'heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God,' Hebrews 9:24. In the new Jerusalem 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The escalation is that the presence once confined to a building is opened to all who are in Him. The silence of the earth before the temple becomes the silence of heaven, Revelation 8:1, before the final acts of judgment.

study.christ:
Habakkuk 2 leads to Christ most plainly by the line the apostles built on. 'The righteous will live by faith' is the sentence on which Paul rests the gospel: 'the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish, just as it is written,' Romans 1:17. In Galatians 3 the argument is shaped to the work of Christ. Paul writes that all who rely on works of the law are under a curse, that 'no one is justified before God by the law, because, "The righteous will live by faith,"' and that 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:10 to 13. The prophet's line explains why that redemption is by trust, and the cross explains why the trust is not misplaced. Habakkuk spoke of a righteous person who lives; Christ is the One by whose death the unrighteous are counted righteous, Romans 3:21 to 26.

It leads to Christ by the person who is coming. Hebrews hears the promise of verse 3 as the coming of the Lord: 'He who is coming will come and will not delay,' Hebrews 10:37. The delay that tried Habakkuk's patience is now the delay between the first coming and the second, and Peter explains it as patience that wants repentance, 2 Peter 3:9. The New Testament never says that Habakkuk saw Jesus by name. It says the pattern of promise and delay he was asked to live by is the pattern of the whole age before Christ returns.

It leads to Christ by the cup. The cup in the LORD's right hand, which comes around to the oppressor, is the cup Jesus knows He must drink. 'Let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. On the cross He takes what the guilty deserve, and Isaiah's promise that the cup of fury will pass from His people becomes real. That is the final answer to the woes: the judgment they announce is not set aside but borne.

It leads to Christ by the filling of the earth with God's glory. Habakkuk says the earth will be filled 'with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.' Paul says that God 'made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6. The very phrase of the prophet is used for the way Christ reveals God. And the hush of verse 20 is turned to worship in Revelation, where the Lamb is in the temple, Revelation 21:22.

It also leads to Christ as the One who Himself lived by faith. Hebrews calls Him 'the author and perfecter of our faith,' Hebrews 12:2, and has Him say, 'I will put My trust in Him,' Hebrews 2:13. The righteous One who trusts the Father through the cross is the pattern and ground of every believer's trust.

A caution is in order. The five woes are not five predictions about Jesus, and the proud one is not a type of Christ. The links lie in the New Testament's own use of verse 4, in the way Hebrews hears verse 3, and in the language of cup, glory and temple that the Gospels and Revelation take up.
study.god:
The central picture of God in this chapter is of One who keeps appointments. The vision has an 'appointed time' and will not lie. God does not answer on the prophet's clock, but He does not forget. His patience is not weakness, and His delay is not denial. Peter says that for the Lord 'a day is like a thousand years,' and that He is 'patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish,' 2 Peter 3:8 to 9. The God of Habakkuk 2 has His own sense of timing, and He asks His people to trust it.

He is the God who answers sin by its own form. The creditor is bitten by creditors. The builder with blood finds his labour fuel for the fire. The one who exposed his neighbours is exposed. This is not arbitrary. It shows that God's judgment is a moral order built into His world, one in which what a person sows comes back to him. 'Will not all of these take up a taunt against him?' means that the very ones he wronged will sing his end.

He is the LORD of Hosts, and verse 13 says that the labour of nations feeds the fire 'from the LORD of Hosts.' The empires strain and weary themselves, and God's will governs the outcome. He is also the God for whom glory is the goal of history. 'The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea' says that the end is not merely the fall of oppressors but the universal knowing of God. The seraphim's cry, 'all the earth is full of His glory,' Isaiah 6:3, becomes a world that sees it.

He is the living God over against the idol. The idol is shaped by hands, cannot speak, has no breath. The LORD speaks, answers, judges, and gives breath. He will not share His glory with another, Isaiah 42:8, and the contrast in verses 18 to 20 sets the made thing beside the Maker. The idol's 'no breath in it at all,' verse 19, is sharpened by Genesis 2:7, where the Maker breathed life into the man He formed.

He is the God who owns the cup. 'The cup in the LORD's right hand' says that the wrath is not wild or random; it is held in a hand, measured, and passed by the Judge. He is also the God who, in the same hand, holds out righteousness by faith. The same One who shames the proud lets the righteous live.

And He is the God before whom silence is the right response. 'The LORD is in His holy temple.' Psalm 11:4 says that the LORD is in His holy temple and on His heavenly throne, with eyes that watch closely. The prophet who accused God of silence is told to be silent himself, and that is not a rebuke. It is the invitation to stand in the awe in which all words fall short.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to write what God says and keep it, to wait for it without losing heart, to live by trust rather than by self, and to be quiet before the One who sits in His temple.

crossReferences.note: Moses tells Israel to write the law 'distinctly' on the stones. The same verb of making plain stands behind Habakkuk 2:2, where the vision is to be clearly inscribed. The word is to have the clarity and the permanence of law.

'Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.' Paul draws on this in Romans 4:3 to show that the principle in Habakkuk 2:4 is the principle by which Abraham was accounted righteous, long before the law.

Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4 as the summary of the gospel. The righteousness of God is revealed in the gospel and is received by faith from start to finish, which is why the proud, who trust themselves, cannot receive it.

Habakkuk 2:4 is set against the law's curse. Christ redeems by becoming a curse, so that the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations through faith. It uses the line to argue that no one is justified by law.

The author quotes Habakkuk 2:3 and 2:4 together and applies them to endurance: 'He who is coming will come and will not delay.' It shows how the delay of the vision becomes the waiting of the church for Christ's return.

The earth 'full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water' is the nearest parallel to Habakkuk 2:14. Habakkuk adds the word glory, and puts the promise in the centre of an oracle of woes.

God removes the cup of staggering from Jerusalem and places it in the hands of her tormentors. It gives the same moral logic as Habakkuk 2:16, where the cup comes around to the one who made others drink, and shows it as a mercy to the afflicted.

The woe on the one who builds a palace by unrighteousness, with wages withheld and innocent blood shed, is nearly the woe of Habakkuk 2:9 to 12. Jeremiah applies the pattern to Judah's king, so the prophets' woes cover the covenant people as well as Babylon.

The song of contempt against the king of Babylon uses the same word for a taunt as Habakkuk 2:6. The nations that were plundered speak a proverb against their plunderer, and the prophets give the taunt the same weight of a divine verdict on a fallen empire.

Idols have mouths that cannot speak and those who make them become like them. It states the point of Habakkuk 2:18 and 19: the creator who trusts his creation becomes as lifeless as the thing he made.

Jesus says that if the crowd keeps silent, the stones will cry out. It picks up the idea in Habakkuk 2:11 of the inanimate order speaking, though in Luke the stones would praise a King rather than testify against a builder.

God 'made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.' It takes the phrase of Habakkuk 2:14 and locates the knowledge of God's glory in the person of Christ.

study.oneStory:
This passage stands at the centre of the book and, in many ways, at the centre of the whole Bible's account of how people are put right with God. The story began with a man and a woman who listened to a voice that said God's word could not be trusted and who reached for what they wanted. The story of the fall is the story of the proud one whose soul is not upright. Habakkuk 2 gives the opposite principle in a single sentence: the righteous will live by faith. What the first couple lost by distrust is recovered by trust.

The principle is not new with Habakkuk. Genesis 15:6 shows Abraham believing the LORD, and it was counted to him as righteousness. The patriarchs lived by promise rather than sight. Habakkuk puts it in a sentence and attaches it to the experience of exile: when the nation is being crushed and the answer is delayed, the way of life is trust. That is how the faithful would get through the exile, and it is why the verse became the key to the New Testament.

The five woes show where the other road leads. They are the story of Babel and Babylon in miniature: build, gain, gather, fill, and fall. In Genesis 11 humanity builds a city to make a name. Here God says that what is built on bloodshed will be consumed. In Revelation 17 and 18 the same city, Babylon the great, collapses in a single hour. The tale of empires from beginning to end is told in these woes.

The passage also sets up the future of Israel's story and the church's. The vision tarries, and the church lives in the tarrying, as Hebrews 10:37 to 39 says. The vision comes in Christ, who bears the cup and rises. The earth begins to be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the gospel goes out, and Paul lives in that spreading.

The end of the story is Habakkuk 2:14 completed. In the new creation, 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3, and God's glory lights the city, so the earth is filled in the fullest sense. The idols are gone, the cup has been drunk, the city of blood has fallen and the holy city has come down. And the hush of verse 20, 'let all the earth be silent before Him,' becomes the quiet of those who see His face, and who then break into the praise of the multitude in Revelation 19:1.

sermon.title: The Just Shall Live by Faith
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly on Habakkuk with 2:4 at the center, drawing out that the righteous live and are kept safe for eternity by faith in God, and connecting it to the gospel of justification by faith. A faithful, orthodox handling of the key verse of this movement.

quiz.q: What is the central statement of God's answer in this chapter?

options.text: The proud one is not upright, but the righteous will live by faith.
options.note: Habakkuk 2:4 is the hinge of the book and the seed of the New Testament gospel.

options.text: The proud will collapse under their arrogance while those who trust God endure.
options.note: A faithful paraphrase, though the exact wording of 2:4 is the key statement.

options.text: That the righteous will live by keeping the law perfectly.
options.note: The text says by faith, which the New Testament sets against justification by works.

options.text: That Babylon will rule forever unchallenged.
options.note: The opposite: Babylon stands under fivefold woe and will fall.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use Habakkuk 2:4?

options.text: Paul and Hebrews quote it for justification by faith and persevering faith, Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, Hebrews 10:38.
options.note: It is one of the most cited Old Testament verses, foundational to the gospel.

options.text: It is used to show that righteousness is received through faith.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it names only part of how the New Testament deploys the verse.

options.text: It is quoted only once, by Jesus, about the temple.
options.note: It is quoted three times in the New Testament, by Paul and in Hebrews.

options.text: It is used to teach salvation by good works.
options.note: It teaches the opposite: the righteous live by faith, not works.

quiz.q: What do the five woes expose?

options.text: The self-destructive sins of the proud oppressor: greed, dishonest gain, bloodshed, cruelty, and idolatry.
options.note: Each woe unmasks a way the arrogant life ruins itself and others.

options.text: God's certain judgment coming on the arrogant and violent.
options.note: True, since a woe announces judgment, but the woes also name the specific sins condemned.

options.text: Minor ceremonial mistakes in worship.
options.note: They address grave moral evils, not small ritual errors.

options.text: God's own supposed injustice.
options.note: The woes are God's just verdict on human wickedness.

quiz.q: What is promised in the refrain of 2:14?

options.text: The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
options.note: The high point of the chapter: God's glory will flood the whole world.

options.text: That one day God's glory will be known across the whole earth.
options.note: A faithful paraphrase, though it drops the vivid image of waters covering the sea.

options.text: That the seas will dry up.
options.note: The waters covering the sea is an image of fullness, not of drought.

options.text: That Babylon's glory will spread over the earth.
options.note: It is the LORD's glory, not the oppressor's, that will fill the earth.

options.text: The LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him.
options.note: A call to reverent silence before the living God, over against lifeless idols.

options.text: With a call to reverent awe before the sovereign, living God.
options.note: This captures the sense, though the actual words are the LORD in His holy temple, let all be silent.

options.text: With a promise that the proud will never be judged.
options.note: The whole section promises sure judgment on the proud.

options.text: With a command to build more idols of gold and silver.
options.note: The passage exposes idols as breathless and worthless.

quiz.q: What does living by faith mean in Habakkuk's own setting?

options.text: Trusting God and His promise to survive the crisis, rather than relying on one's own strength.
options.note: The righteous lean on God while they wait for the vision to come.

options.text: Waiting patiently for God to act instead of taking matters into one's own hands.
options.note: True and part of it, but the core is active trust in God and His promise.

options.text: Pretending the danger from Babylon does not exist.
options.note: Faith is not denial; it is trust in God amid real danger.

options.text: Earning God's favor through hard work.
options.note: It is trust in God, not achievement, that marks the righteous.

questions: God told Habakkuk to write the vision and wait, because it would surely come. Where are you being called to trust God's timing when His promise seems to linger?
The righteous will live by faith is the line the whole gospel hangs on. In plain terms, are you resting for your standing with God on your own performance or on faith in Christ?
The proud man's appetite was never satisfied. Where do you see the endless, restless hunger of pride or greed in your own heart, and how does trusting God free you from it?
The five woes show how sins like exploitation and idolatry destroy those who practice them. Is there any small idol or dishonest gain you are tolerating that God is calling you to abandon?
One day the earth will be filled with the knowledge of God's glory. How would living in the light of that certain future change your priorities this week?

translationNotes.note: The Septuagint and Hebrews 10:37 read the coming one personally, though he lingers, wait for him, since he will surely come; the Hebrew reads it of the vision. Either way the certainty and timing are the point.
The Hebrew emunah can be rendered faith or faithfulness; the BSB footnote notes the verse is cited in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, and Hebrews 10:38.
The Dead Sea Scrolls read wealth where the Masoretic Text reads wine; the BSB follows the Scrolls. The sense is that ill-gotten gain betrays the arrogant man.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, Septuagint, and Syriac read and stagger where the Masoretic Text reads and expose your uncircumcision; both convey the shame poured out on the oppressor.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Habakkuk 2:2-20. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose within each verse.
